title: Study Finds 'Hidden' Sleep Crisis Among Workers over 50
paragraphs: Around one in three workers in the UK is over the age of 50. Now, a new study suggests that many of these older workers may be experiencing serious sleep problems without realizing it, and that their jobs may be partly to blame.

The study was carried out by researchers at the University of Edinburgh as part of a program called Supporting Healthy Ageing at Work, and it was published in the journal Scientific Reports in July 2026. It was led by Athanasios Tsanas, a professor of digital health and data science.

The researchers followed 45 workers aged between 50 and 66 from a range of industries for a whole year. During that time, the participants completed more than 1,900 questionnaires about their well-being and their experiences at work. They also wore devices on their wrists that tracked their sleep, providing more than 5,200 days of data. The researchers then used artificial intelligence to identify the factors most strongly linked to poor sleep and well-being.

The results were striking. Nearly 70% of the participants experienced persistent, clinically significant sleep problems, even though none of them had a known history of sleep disorders. In addition, almost 92% met the medical threshold for a sleep disorder at least once during the study.

Interestingly, many participants believed that they were simply not getting enough sleep. However, the data from the wrist devices told a different story. Although most participants slept between 6.5 and 8 hours a night on average, 90% experienced disturbed sleep. In other words, the real problem was often waking up frequently during the night, rather than sleeping too little.

The researchers found that stress at work was one of the main factors linked to poor sleep and lower well-being. Feeling gloomy, irritable or tense at work was linked to lower well-being, regardless of gender or industry. On the other hand, a better work-life balance and greater job satisfaction were linked to better well-being. According to Dr. Belinda Steffan, another researcher on the project, other factors such as menopause, aging, caring for family members and financial stress may also play a role.
Tsanas said the analysis clearly shows that many of these sleep and well-being problems are related to work. However, the study was small, so the results need to be confirmed in larger groups.
